claims.label: Foreclosure / Deficiency Judgment
claims.note: This is the legal deficiency the court would enter judgment for, not a prediction of what will actually be collected. Whether a judgment is ultimately collectable depends heavily on the borrower/guarantor's post-judgment asset picture and is outside the scope of this calculator -- treat this figure as case value, not a collection forecast. Texas's deficiency-judgment rules were applied (Tex. Prop. Code §§ 51.003–51.005). Procedural trap to flag: Deficiency suit generally must be filed within 2 years of the foreclosure sale. A fair-value offset applies here (the credit against the debt is the greater of sale proceeds or a court-determined fair value) -- enter a fair-value figure if one has been determined and it exceeds the sale proceeds, which would reduce this deficiency.

claims.label: Receivership Grant/Denial
claims.note: Not a dollar claim -- operational-control relief. Sample has grown to 10 real matters; of the 8 with a reported ruling, 7 resulted in a receiver appointed and 1 (Brick Air Capital v. NLD Props.) was denied outright even with a consent-to-receivership clause, on the court's equitable discretion.

claims.label: Lender Liability (borrower-asserted)
claims.note: Historically borrower-unfriendly absent clear bad faith; recent real cases trend toward procedural wins rather than dollar outcomes. Damages, if any, are typically limited to contract damages and out-of-pocket costs.

claims.label: Attorney's Fees
claims.note: Posture-tiered flat-dollar estimate (went to trial) -- fees are driven by procedural effort, not claim size, for a typical matter in this range; a large or unusually complex matter can run higher.

extractedFacts.foreclosureProcedureTrap: Deficiency suit generally must be filed within 2 years of the foreclosure sale.
extractedFacts.foreclosureStateNote: Unlike California, Texas's dominant non-judicial power-of-sale method does NOT waive deficiency rights. Either party may request the court determine the property's fair market value; the sale price is presumed to equal fair market value unless rebutted by competent evidence, in which case the higher fair-value figure controls the deficiency calculation.

outcome.description: After a two-day bench trial the court awarded Brandon $245,109.20 in actual damages against Wells Fargo and Midland jointly and severally, plus $245,109.20 in exemplary damages against each of them ($735,327.60 total damages), and $125,000 in attorney's fees plus conditional appellate fees; it found no consequential damages. The Thirteenth Court of Appeals reversed the judgment against Midland entirely and the exemplary damages, and affirmed the rest, leaving $245,109.20 in actual damages against Wells Fargo plus the fee award.
outcome.finalNote: Modified on appeal: exemplary damages and Midland liability reversed; actual damages affirmed.
